vtrmc-1983-01.title: Count exponent triples
vtrmc-1983-01.body:
Expanding $(a+b+c)^n$ and collecting like terms gives $\sum\frac{n!}{i!\,j!\,k!}a^ib^jc^k$ over all triples of non-negative integers with $i+j+k=n$; every coefficient is positive, so each such triple gives one term and no terms cancel.

For fixed $i\in\{0,\dots,n\}$ there are $n-i+1$ choices of $(j,k)$ with $j+k=n-i$. So the number of terms is
$$\sum_{i=0}^n(n-i+1)=(n+1)+n+\cdots+1=\frac{(n+1)(n+2)}2 .$$
**Answer: $\dfrac{(n+1)(n+2)}{2}$.**

vtrmc-1983-01.title: Stars and bars / induction
vtrmc-1983-01.body:
*Stars and bars:* triples $(i,j,k)$ of non-negative integers with $i+j+k=n$ correspond to arrangements of $n$ stars and $2$ bars, so there are $\binom{n+2}2$ of them.

*Induction view:* $(a+b+c)^n=\sum_{i=0}^n\binom ni a^i(b+c)^{n-i}$, and $(b+c)^{n-i}$ has $n-i+1$ terms by the given fact; the terms for different $i$ are different (different powers of $a$). Total $\sum_{i}(n-i+1)=\binom{n+2}{2}$. (Check: $n=1$ gives $3$ terms $a,b,c$; $n=2$ gives $6$.)

vtrmc-1983-02.title: Pair each number with its complement
vtrmc-1983-02.body:
Let $N=d_1d_2\dots d_m$ (digits, $d_1\neq0$). Then $R(C(N))$ has digits $9-d_m,\,9-d_{m-1},\dots,9-d_1$, so $N$ is special iff
$$d_i+d_{m+1-i}=9\qquad\text{for all }i.$$
If $m$ were odd, the middle digit would satisfy $2d=9$, impossible; so $m\in\{2,4,6\}$ (as $N<10^6$). The last digit $d_m\notin\{0,9\}$ is equivalent to $d_1=9-d_m\in\{1,\dots,8\}$. So a special number of length $m=2j$ is determined by its first $j$ digits: $d_1\in\{1,\dots,8\}$ and $d_2,\dots,d_j$ arbitrary. There are $8\cdot10^{j-1}$ of them.

*Pairing.* If $N$ (of length $m$) is special with $d_1\in\{1..8\}$, so is $N'=(10^m-1)-N$, whose digits are $9-d_i$ (still satisfying the symmetry condition, with first digit $9-d_1\in\{1..8\}$). $N'\neq N$ (as $d_1\neq 9-d_1$), so the special numbers of length $m$ split into pairs with sum $10^m-1$.

* $m=2$: $8$ numbers, sum $4\cdot99=396$.
* $m=4$: $80$ numbers, sum $40\cdot9999=399\,960$.
* $m=6$: $800$ numbers, sum $400\cdot999\,999=399\,999\,600$.

Total: $396+399\,960+399\,999\,600=400\,399\,956$.

**Answer: $400399956$.**

vtrmc-1983-02.title: Sum digit by digit
vtrmc-1983-02.body:
For $m=2j$ the number is $\sum_{i=1}^m d_i10^{m-i}$ with $d_{m+1-i}=9-d_i$. Over all $8\cdot10^{j-1}$ special numbers of length $m$: the first digit $d_1$ averages $4.5$ (values $1..8$), each other free digit averages $4.5$ (values $0..9$), and hence every digit position (including the determined ones, which equal $9$ minus a free digit) averages $4.5$. So the average special number of length $m$ is $4.5\cdot\underbrace{11\ldots1}_{m}=\frac{10^m-1}{2}$, and the sum is $8\cdot10^{j-1}\cdot\frac{10^m-1}{2}$:
$$m=2:\ 8\cdot\tfrac{99}2=396,\quad m=4:\ 80\cdot\tfrac{9999}2=399\,960,\quad m=6:\ 800\cdot\tfrac{999\,999}2=399\,999\,600 .$$
Total $400\,399\,956$ (a computer search over all $N<10^6$ confirms it).

**Answer: $400399956$.**

vtrmc-1983-03.title: Parallelograms and the centroid
vtrmc-1983-03.body:
(In (b), "$\triangle OAQ$" is a misprint for $\triangle OAB$.) Assume the triangle is non-degenerate ($ac\neq0$); let $T$ be its area.

**(a)** Let $P=A+B-O=(a+b,\,c)$, the fourth vertex of the parallelogram $OAPB$. A diagonal splits a parallelogram into two triangles of equal area, so
* diagonal $OP$: $\text{area}(OAP)=\text{area}(OBP)=\tfrac12\text{area}(OAPB)$;
* diagonal $AB$: $\text{area}(ABP)=\text{area}(ABO)=T=\tfrac12\text{area}(OAPB)$.

So all three areas equal $T$, and $P$ is outside the triangle (it lies on the other side of $AB$ from $O$). By the same argument $O+A-B=(a-b,-c)$ and $O+B-A=(b-a,c)$ also work.

**(b)** Let $Q=G=\left(\frac{a+b}3,\frac c3\right)$, the centroid. The heights of $OAG$, $OBG$, $ABG$ over the sides $OA$, $OB$, $AB$ are one third of the corresponding heights of the triangle (the centroid divides each median in the ratio $2:1$, so its distance to a side is $\frac13$ of the opposite vertex's distance). Hence each of the three areas is $T/3$. For instance $\text{area}(OAG)=\frac12|a|\cdot\frac{|c|}{3}=\frac T3$.

These are in fact the only solutions — see the second approach. ∎

vtrmc-1983-03.title: Barycentric coordinates: all solutions
vtrmc-1983-03.body:
Write any point as $P=\alpha O+\beta A+\gamma B$ with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=1$. Then (signed areas are affine in $P$)
$$\text{area}(ABP)=|\alpha|T,\qquad \text{area}(OBP)=|\beta|T,\qquad\text{area}(OAP)=|\gamma|T .$$
(Indeed $\text{area}(OAP)$ is $\frac12|OA|\cdot\text{dist}(P,OA)$, and the distance of $P$ to line $OA$ is $|\gamma|$ times that of $B$.)

Equal areas means $|\alpha|=|\beta|=|\gamma|=t$ with $\alpha+\beta+\gamma=1$. Either all three have the same sign: $3t=1$, giving the centroid $(\frac13,\frac13,\frac13)$, the unique **interior** point; or one sign differs: $t+t-t=1$, $t=1$, giving $(1,1,-1)$, $(1,-1,1)$, $(-1,1,1)$, i.e.
$$O+A-B=(a-b,-c),\qquad O+B-A=(b-a,c),\qquad A+B-O=(a+b,c),$$
the three **exterior** solutions. ∎

vtrmc-1983-04.title: Pigeonhole on degrees
vtrmc-1983-04.body:
"Directly connected" is a symmetric relation on the towns, i.e. a simple graph, and $f(T_k)$ is the degree of $T_k$: the number of towns $T_j\neq T_k$ directly connected to it. So $0\le f(T_k)\le n-1$.

Suppose $f$ were one-to-one. Then the $n$ values $f(T_1),\dots,f(T_n)$ would be $n$ distinct numbers in $\{0,1,\dots,n-1\}$, hence exactly $0,1,\dots,n-1$. So some town $T_p$ has $f(T_p)=n-1$ — it is directly connected to every other town — and some town $T_q$ has $f(T_q)=0$ — it is directly connected to no town. Since $n\ge2$, $p\neq q$, and $T_p$ is directly connected to $T_q$, contradicting $f(T_q)=0$.

Hence two towns have the same value of $f$: $f$ is not one-to-one. ∎

vtrmc-1983-04.title: Case split on isolated towns
vtrmc-1983-04.body:
* If some town is directly connected to no other town, then every town is connected to at most the $n-2$ towns other than itself and that isolated one, so all values of $f$ lie in $\{0,1,\dots,n-2\}$.
* Otherwise every town has $f\ge1$, so all values lie in $\{1,2,\dots,n-1\}$.

Either way the $n$ towns take at most $n-1$ different values, so by the pigeonhole principle two towns share a value, and $f$ is not one-to-one. ∎

vtrmc-1983-05.title: Differentiate and separate variables
vtrmc-1983-05.body:
Assume $f$ is continuously differentiable (so that arc length is $\int\sqrt{1+f'^2}$) and $f\ge0$ (the area lies above the $x$-axis). The condition is
$$\int_0^Lf(x)\,dx=\int_0^L\sqrt{1+f'(x)^2}\,dx\qquad(L\ge0).$$
Differentiating with respect to $L$ (fundamental theorem of calculus):
$$f(x)=\sqrt{1+f'(x)^2}\qquad(x\ge0),$$
and conversely this ODE implies the condition (both sides vanish at $L=0$). So $f\ge1$ and $f'^2=f^2-1$.

*Where $f>1$:* on an interval where $f>1$, $f'$ is continuous and never $0$, so it has a constant sign, and
$$\frac{d}{dx}\cosh^{-1}f(x)=\frac{f'(x)}{\sqrt{f(x)^2-1}}=\pm1 .$$
Hence $\cosh^{-1}f(x)=\pm(x+C)$, i.e. $f(x)=\cosh(x+C)$ ($\cosh$ is even).

*Check:* for $f(x)=\cosh(x+C)$, $\sqrt{1+\sinh^2(x+C)}=\cosh(x+C)=f(x)$ ✓ — and this works on all of $[0,\infty)$ for every real $C$ (if $C<0$ the graph first goes down to the value $1$ at $x=-C$ and then up). The constant $f\equiv1$ also works ($f'=0$, $\sqrt{1}=1$).

*All solutions.* The set where $f>1$ is relatively open in $[0,\infty)$; on each of its component intervals $f=\cosh(x+C)$ for one constant $C$, and at an end point of the component lying in $(0,\infty)$ we have $f=1$ by continuity, which forces that end point to be $-C$. A component cannot have two such end points (they would both equal $-C$), so there is at most a component $[0,p)$ and at most a component $(q,\infty)$, and $f=1$ on $[p,q]$ in between. So $f$ is $\cosh$-shaped, possibly with a flat piece $f=1$ inserted: for some $0\le p\le q\le\infty$,
$$f(x)=\begin{cases}\cosh(x-p),&0\le x\le p\\ 1,&p\le x\le q\\ \cosh(x-q),&x\ge q\end{cases}$$
or $f(x)=\cosh(x+C)$ with $C>0$. (These pieces join with matching values and zero slope, so $f$ is $C^1$.) The natural answer, and the one with no flat piece, is
$$f(x)=\cosh(x+C),\quad\text{e.g. } f(x)=\cosh x .$$

vtrmc-1983-05.title: Verify the catenary directly
vtrmc-1983-05.body:
For $f(x)=\cosh(x+C)$:
$$\text{area}=\int_0^L\cosh(x+C)\,dx=\sinh(L+C)-\sinh C,$$
$$\text{arc length}=\int_0^L\sqrt{1+\sinh^2(x+C)}\,dx=\int_0^L\cosh(x+C)\,dx=\sinh(L+C)-\sinh C .$$
They agree for every $L\ge0$. So the catenary $y=\cosh(x+C)$ (in particular $y=\cosh x$) has the required property; the first approach shows that, apart from the trivial solution $y\equiv1$ and pieces glued to it, these are the only ones.

vtrmc-1983-06.title: $f\circ g$ has order 3
vtrmc-1983-06.body:
(The composites are understood as formulas, i.e. as linear fractional maps; strictly speaking $g$ is only defined on $(0,1)$ while $f$ maps $(0,1)$ onto $(1,\infty)$.)

Every function of the given form is $h_k=(f\circ g)^k\circ f$ for some $k\ge0$ (or $k\ge1$; it does not matter below). Let $\varphi=f\circ g$:
$$\varphi(x)=\frac1{1-x},\qquad \varphi^2(x)=\frac1{1-\frac1{1-x}}=\frac{1-x}{-x}=\frac{x-1}{x},\qquad \varphi^3(x)=\varphi\!\left(\frac{x-1}{x}\right)=\frac1{1-\frac{x-1}x}=x .$$
So $\varphi^3=\mathrm{id}$ and $h_k$ depends only on $k\bmod3$:
* $h_0=f$: $\ \dfrac1x=\dfrac{0x+1}{1x+0}$;
* $h_1=\varphi\circ f$: $\ \dfrac1{1-\frac1x}=\dfrac{x}{x-1}=\dfrac{1x+0}{1x-1}$;
* $h_2=\varphi^2\circ f$: $\ \dfrac{\frac1x-1}{\frac1x}=1-x=\dfrac{-1x+1}{0x+1}$.

These three are distinct (at $x=\frac12$ they take the values $2,\,-1,\,\frac12$), and every composite of the given form equals one of them (also when at least one $g$ is required, since $h_3=f$). ∎

vtrmc-1983-06.title: Matrices
vtrmc-1983-06.body:
Represent $\frac{ax+b}{cx+d}$ by $\begin{pmatrix}a&b\\c&d\end{pmatrix}$ (up to a nonzero factor); composition is matrix multiplication. $F=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\1&0\end{pmatrix}$, $G=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\0&1\end{pmatrix}$, so
$$FG=\begin{pmatrix}0&1\\-1&1\end{pmatrix},\quad (FG)^2=\begin{pmatrix}-1&1\\-1&0\end{pmatrix},\quad (FG)^3=\begin{pmatrix}-1&0\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}=-I .$$
Hence the composites $(FG)^kF$ give only $F$, $FGF=\begin{pmatrix}1&0\\1&-1\end{pmatrix}$ and $(FG)^2F=\begin{pmatrix}1&-1\\0&-1\end{pmatrix}$, i.e. $\frac1x$, $\frac x{x-1}$, $\frac{x-1}{-1}=1-x$ — the same three functions.

vtrmc-1983-07.title: Vieta's formulas
vtrmc-1983-07.body:
*Remark on the statement.* For $a=b=0$ the equation $x^4=0$ has only the real root $0$ (with multiplicity $4$), so the statement must be read as "unless $a=b=0$". We prove: if $(a,b)\neq(0,0)$, not all roots are real.

Let $r_1,r_2,r_3,r_4$ be the roots (with multiplicity) and suppose they are all real. The polynomial $x^4+0x^3+0x^2+ax+b$ gives by Vieta's formulas
$$\sum_i r_i=0,\qquad\sum_{i<j}r_ir_j=0 .$$
Hence
$$\sum_i r_i^2=\Big(\sum_i r_i\Big)^2-2\sum_{i<j}r_ir_j=0 .$$
A sum of squares of real numbers is $0$ only if all are $0$, so $r_1=r_2=r_3=r_4=0$ and the polynomial is $x^4$, i.e. $a=b=0$. So for $(a,b)\ne(0,0)$ the equation has a non-real root. ∎

vtrmc-1983-07.title: Rolle's theorem
vtrmc-1983-07.body:
Let $p(x)=x^4+ax+b$ and suppose all four roots (with multiplicity) are real. By Rolle's theorem (between distinct roots) together with the fact that a root of multiplicity $m$ of $p$ is a root of multiplicity $m-1$ of $p'$, the derivative $p'(x)=4x^3+a$ then has three real roots counted with multiplicity.

But $4x^3+a$ has only one real root, $x=-\sqrt[3]{a/4}$, and it is simple unless $a=0$. So $a=0$, and $p(x)=x^4+b$. If $b>0$ it has no real root; if $b<0$ its roots are $\pm|b|^{1/4}$ and $\pm i|b|^{1/4}$. Only $b=0$ remains. Hence, except for the trivial case $a=b=0$, $x^4+ax+b=0$ cannot have only real roots. ∎

vtrmc-1983-08.title: Find a linear recurrence
vtrmc-1983-08.body:
The first terms are $1,1,1,2,3,7,11,26,41,97,\dots$

*Positivity.* By induction all $f_n>0$ (the recurrence divides a positive number by a positive number), so the sequence is well defined.

*A conserved ratio.* For $n\ge3$ we have both
$$f_{n+1}f_{n-2}=f_nf_{n-1}+1\qquad\text{and}\qquad f_nf_{n-3}=f_{n-1}f_{n-2}+1 .$$
Subtracting,
$$f_{n+1}f_{n-2}-f_nf_{n-3}=f_nf_{n-1}-f_{n-1}f_{n-2},\quad\text{i.e.}\quad f_{n-2}\,(f_{n+1}+f_{n-1})=f_n\,(f_{n-1}+f_{n-3}).$$
Define $r_k=\dfrac{f_{k+1}+f_{k-1}}{f_k}$ for $k\ge1$. The identity says $r_n=r_{n-2}$ for all $n\ge3$. Since
$$r_1=\frac{f_2+f_0}{f_1}=2,\qquad r_2=\frac{f_3+f_1}{f_2}=\frac{2+1}{1}=3,$$
we get $r_k=2$ for odd $k$ and $r_k=3$ for even $k$. Therefore, for all $k\ge1$,
$$f_{k+1}=r_kf_k-f_{k-1}\quad\text{with } r_k\in\{2,3\}.$$

*Integrality.* $f_0,f_1,f_2$ are integers, and if $f_{k-1},f_k$ are integers then so is $f_{k+1}=r_kf_k-f_{k-1}$. By induction every $f_n$ is an integer. ∎

(Check: $f_4=2\cdot2-1=3$, $f_5=3\cdot3-2=7$, $f_6=2\cdot7-3=11$, $f_7=3\cdot11-7=26$, $f_8=2\cdot26-11=41$, all agreeing with the original recurrence, e.g. $f_8=\frac{26\cdot11+1}{7}=41$.)

vtrmc-1983-08.title: Eliminate the parity: one recurrence
vtrmc-1983-08.body:
With $r_k=\frac{f_{k+1}+f_{k-1}}{f_k}$ as in the first approach ($r_{k}r_{k+1}=6$ for every $k$, since consecutive indices have opposite parity), for $k\ge2$:
$$f_{k+2}+2f_k+f_{k-2}=(f_{k+2}+f_k)+(f_k+f_{k-2})=r_{k+1}f_{k+1}+r_{k-1}f_{k-1}=r_{k+1}(f_{k+1}+f_{k-1})=r_{k+1}r_kf_k=6f_k,$$
using $r_{k-1}=r_{k+1}$. Hence the single parity-free recurrence
$$f_{k+2}=4f_k-f_{k-2}\qquad(k\ge2)$$
(e.g. $f_4=4f_2-f_0=3$, $f_5=4f_3-f_1=7$, $f_6=4f_4-f_2=11$). With the integer starting values $f_0,f_1,f_2,f_3=1,1,1,2$ it shows again that every $f_n$ is an integer. (An exact rational-arithmetic computation of the original recurrence for the first $40$ terms confirms that no fractions appear.) ∎
